## Variables in go (most of the below text were generated by AI, lol it was fun)

variables in go can be package-level or function-level. Package-level variables are declared outside of any function and 
are accessible throughout the package, while function-level variables are declared within a function and 
are only accessible within that function.

- simple declaration of a variable in go is done using the var keyword followed by the variable name and type.
e.g.:
	var i int

- when declaring multiple variables of the same type, we can use a single var statement with a comma-separated list of variable names.
e.g.: 
	var i, j, k int

- we can omit the type of a variable when declaring it, and go will infer the type based on the value assigned to it.
e.g.: 
	var i = 10 // i is inferred to be of type int

- multiple variables can also be declared and initialized in a single var statement.
e.g.: 
	var i, j, k = 10, 20, 30 // i, j, and k are inferred to be of type int

- we can also use the short variable declaration syntax := to declare and initialize a variable in one line.
e.g.: 
	i := 10 // i is inferred to be of type int

- multiple variables can also be declared and initialized using the short variable declaration syntax.
e.g.: 
	i, j, k := 10, 20, 30 // i, j, and k are inferred to be of type int

- constants in go are declared using the const keyword followed by the constant name and value.
e.g.: 
	const pi = 3.14

- we can also declare multiple constants in a single const statement.
e.g.: 
	const (
		pi = 3.14
		e  = 2.71
	)	

- go also supports typed constants, where we can specify the type of the constant.
e.g.: 
	const pi float64 = 3.14

- we can also declare multiple typed constants in a single const statement.
e.g.: 
	const (
		pi float64 = 3.14
		e  float64 = 2.71
	)

- go also supports iota, which is a special constant that can be used to create enumerated constants.
e.g.: 
	const (
		a = iota // a is 0
		b        // b is 1
		c        // c is 2
	)
	
- we can also use iota to create a sequence of constants with a specific pattern.
e.g.:
	const (
		a = iota * 2 // a is 0
		b            // b is 2
		c            // c is 4
	)

- go also supports untyped constants, which can be used in expressions without specifying a type.
e.g.: 
	const pi = 3.14 // pi is an untyped constant

- we can also use untyped constants in expressions without specifying a type.
e.g.: 
	const pi = 3.14
	var radius float64 = 5.0
	var area = pi * radius * radius // area is inferred to be of type float64

- go also supports variable shadowing, where a variable declared in an inner scope can have the same name as a variable declared in an outer scope.
e.g.: 
	var x int = 10
	func example() {
		var x int = 20 // this x shadows the outer x
		fmt.Println(x) // prints 20
	}

- go also supports variable initialization with zero values, where a variable is automatically initialized to its zero value if it is not explicitly initialized.
e.g.: 
	var i int // i is initialized to 0
	var s string // s is initialized to ""
	var b bool // b is initialized to false

- go also supports variable initialization with default values, where a variable can be initialized with a default value if it is not explicitly initialized.
e.g.: 
	var i int = 10 // i is initialized to 10
	var s string = "hello" // s is initialized to "hello"
	var b bool = true // b is initialized to true	

- go also supports variable initialization with composite literals, where a variable can be initialized with a composite literal such as an array, slice, map, or struct.
e.g.: 
	var arr = [3]int{1, 2, 3} // arr is initialized to an array of 3 integers
	var slice = []int{1, 2, 3} // slice is initialized to a slice of integers
	var m = map[string]int{"a": 1, "b": 2} // m is initialized to a map of string keys and int values
	var s = struct{ name string }{name: "John"} // s is initialized to a struct with a name field

# basic types in go

- go has several basic types, including:
	- bool: represents a boolean value (true or false)
	- string: represents a sequence of characters
	- int: represents a signed integer (int  int8  int16  int32  int64)
	- uint: represents an unsigned integer (uint  uint8  uint16  uint32  uint64  uintptr)
	- float32: represents a 32-bit floating-point number 
	- float64: represents a 64-bit floating-point number
	- complex64: represents a complex number with float32 real and imaginary parts
	- complex128: represents a complex number with float64 real and imaginary parts
	- byte: represents an 8-bit unsigned integer (alias for uint8)
	- rune: represents a Unicode code point (alias for int32)
	- go also has several composite types, including:
	- array: represents a fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type
	- slice: represents a variable-size sequence of elements of the same type
	- map: represents a collection of key-value pairs
	- struct: represents a collection of fields with different types
	- pointer: represents a memory address of a value
